title: The first programmable computers
matchup: ENIAC (1945–1946) and Turing-related accounts vs Zuse’s Z3 (1941) and Flowers’s Colossus (1943–1944)
question: Do the documented capabilities of Z3, Colossus and ENIAC support Schmidhuber's proposed division of first-computer credit?

usual_credit.summary: Standard computing histories do not assign every first to one machine: they distinguish programmability, general-purpose operation, electronic construction and stored programs. The [Computer History Museum](https://www.computerhistory.org/revolution/birth-of-the-computer/4/78) credits the ENIAC project with a large-scale computer operating at electronic speed, while separately recording Zuse's earlier relay-based Z3. The [National Museum of Computing](https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus) credits Colossus with digital, programmable electronic operation but describes its purpose and programmability as limited; Turing's abstract machine is a separate theoretical contribution, not the same physical machine.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber credits Zuse with the first working programmable general-purpose computer and argues that Zuse's engineering did not depend on Turing's 1936 paper. He distinguishes the electromechanical Z3 from electronic special-purpose machines, and in a 2006 letter challenged a Nature timeline that began with ENIAC instead of Colossus. In later posts he also argues that Z3's missing conditional-jump instruction does not prevent universality when its arithmetic operations and an idealized memory model are considered.

The first general purpose computer was completed by Konrad Zuse in 1941

response.summary: The [German Patent and Trade Mark Office](https://dpma.de/english/our_office/publications/milestones/computerpioneers/konradzuse/index.html) credits Z3 as a functioning freely programmable binary computer while stressing that modern computers have several inventors. The [National Museum of Computing](https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus) distinguishes Colossus's limited programmability from later stored-program machines, and the Computer History Museum describes ENIAC's contribution in large-scale electronic computation. These institutional accounts divide credit by capability and construction rather than choosing one machine for every first. They are historical comparisons, not replies accepting or rejecting every claim in Schmidhuber's articles about Zuse or Turing.

quotes.text: Colossus was preceded by several computers, many of them being a first in some category.

agreed_facts: Zuse completed the relay-based Z3 in 1941: https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/1941
ENIAC was built between 1943 and 1945 and initially programmed through configurations of wires and switches: https://www.computerhistory.org/revolution/birth-of-the-computer/4/78
Flowers's Colossus was working at Bletchley Park in February 1944 and had limited programmability for a cryptanalytic task: https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus
crux: The question is which criteria a first-computer claim includes, rather than whether Z3 preceded ENIAC. A mathematical universality result for an idealized Z3, a working general-purpose calculator, an electronic special-purpose machine and a stored-program computer establish different kinds of priority.
